q: The attractive forces that hold atoms together in compounds are also known as _____.
e: Chemical bonds are the attractive forces that hold atoms together in compounds.

q: In atoms, the main shells can be divided into s, p, d, and f subshells which can be filled with _____ electrons, respectively.
e: The s, p, d, and f subshells can hold a maximum of 2, 6, 10, and 14 electrons respectively.

q: The s subshell has only one _____ orbital.
e: The s subshell contains only one spherical-shaped orbital.

q: There are three _____ p orbitals ($p_x, p_y, p_z$).
e: The p subshell consists of three dumbbell-shaped orbitals.

q: The five d orbitals have _____ shapes.
e: The five d orbitals are characterised by double dumbbell shapes.

q: According to the _____ principle, electrons are filled in the lower energy atomic orbitals before filling higher energy ones.
e: The Aufbau principle states that electrons fill lower energy atomic orbitals before higher energy ones.

q: Pauli's exclusion principle states that no more than _____ electrons can occupy the same orbital.
e: Pauli's exclusion principle limits an orbital to a maximum of two electrons.

q: Two electrons in the same orbital must have _____ spins.
e: Electrons sharing the same orbital must possess opposite spins.

q: Hund's rule states that every orbital in a subshell is singly occupied with one electron before any one orbital is _____.
e: Hund's rule dictates that orbitals in a subshell are singly occupied before any is doubly occupied.

q: The electrons in the valence shells of an atom are known as the _____ electrons.
e: Valence electrons are located in the outermost shell of an atom.

q: For an atom, the number of valence electrons is equal to its _____ in the Periodic Table.
e: An element's group number corresponds to its number of valence electrons.

q: Atoms lose, gain, or share electrons in order to achieve the stable electronic structures of noble gases, which is known as the _____ rule.
e: The octet rule describes the tendency of atoms to achieve eight electrons in their valence shell.

q: The octet rule does not apply to _____ elements.
e: The octet rule has exceptions and does not apply to d-block elements.

q: Electronegativity is a measure of the ability of an atom to attract the _____ to itself.
e: Electronegativity measures an atom's ability to attract shared electrons in a chemical bond.

q: Electron affinity is the amount of energy _____ when an electron is added to a gaseous atom.
e: Electron affinity is defined as the energy released upon adding an electron to a gaseous atom.

q: Ionisation energy is the amount of energy required to _____ an electron from a gaseous atom.
e: Ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom.

q: Generally, the higher the first ionisation energy of an element, the _____ is its electronegativity.
e: Elements with high ionisation energy tightly hold their electrons, correlating with greater electronegativity.

q: There are _____ main types of chemical bonding.
e: The three main types of chemical bonding are ionic, covalent, and metallic.

q: The hydrogen bond is the strongest intermolecular force followed by _____ forces.
e: Hydrogen bonds are the strongest intermolecular forces, followed by van der Waals forces.

q: Among van der Waals forces, _____ forces are the weakest intermolecular forces that can be found in all substances.
e: London dispersion forces are the weakest intermolecular forces and exist in all substances.

q: Most bonds are not 100% ionic or 100% covalent, instead most bonds have at least some degree of _____ character.
e: Most chemical bonds possess a mixture of both ionic and covalent character.

q: The outermost shell electrons of atoms are the basis for understanding the joining of atoms, and this interaction leads to the forces of attraction known as _____.
e: The interaction of valence electrons leads to chemical bonds that hold atoms together.

q: Elements having high electron affinity easily gain electrons, resulting in the formation of the _____.
e: Gaining electrons results in the formation of negatively charged anions.

q: Elements having low ionisation energy easily lose electrons, resulting in the formation of the _____.
e: Losing electrons results in the formation of positively charged cations.

q: Ionic bonding results from the _____ of electrons from one atom to another.
e: Ionic bonding is formed by the complete transfer of valence electrons.

q: Ionic bonding mostly takes place when the difference in electronegativity is greater than _____.
e: An electronegativity difference greater than 1.8 typically indicates ionic bonding.

q: Ionic bonding generally occurs between reactive metals and reactive _____.
e: Ionic bonds typically form between reactive metals and reactive non-metals.

q: When an ionic bond forms, a metal loses electrons to form positively charged ions known as _____.
e: Metals lose electrons to form positively charged cations.

q: The number of lost or gained electrons by an atom during ionic bonding is the same as the _____ of that element.
e: The number of electrons transferred corresponds to the valency of the element.

q: In the formation of sodium chloride, the difference in electronegativity between Na (0.9) and Cl (3.0) is _____.
e: The difference between 3.0 and 0.9 is 2.1, confirming the ionic nature of NaCl.

q: In the case of magnesium oxide, the electronegativity difference between Mg (1.2) and oxygen (3.5) is _____.
e: The electronegativity difference between oxygen (3.5) and magnesium (1.2) is 2.3.

q: In general, the greater the charge on the ions, the greater the electrostatic attraction and the _____ the ionic bond will be.
e: Higher ionic charges lead to stronger electrostatic attractions and stronger ionic bonds.

q: The melting points of the ionic compounds with the greater charge on the ions are _____.
e: Stronger ionic bonds resulting from greater charges require more energy to break, leading to higher melting points.

q: In solid ionic compounds, their ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move, and hence they cannot conduct _____.
e: Solid ionic compounds cannot conduct electricity because their ions are fixed in the lattice.

q: The crystalline structure of an ionic solid is called a crystal lattice, created by repeating _____.
e: A crystal lattice is formed by the continuous repetition of unit cells.

q: The cubic unit cell can have three types: simple cubic, face-centred cubic, and _____ cubic.
e: The three types of cubic unit cells are simple, face-centred, and body-centred.

q: Sodium chloride has a cubic structure and is formed by repeating the _____ unit cell.
e: The crystal lattice of sodium chloride is based on a face-centred cubic unit cell.

q: In a sodium chloride crystal lattice, each $Na^+$ ion has _____ neighbouring $Cl^-$ ions.
e: Each sodium ion is surrounded by six chloride ions in the NaCl lattice.

q: The term _____ number is used to express the number of ions surrounding the central ion in the lattice.
e: Coordination number defines the number of nearest neighbour ions in a crystal lattice.

q: Since the coordination ratio of $Na^+$ ion to $Cl^-$ ion is 6:6, the simple ratio of 1:1 gives the formula unit of sodium chloride which is _____.
e: The 1:1 ratio of ions yields the formula unit NaCl.

q: A simple cubic unit cell is a cubic cell with an atom in each _____ of the cube.
e: A simple cubic unit cell contains atoms only at the eight corners of the cube.

q: A face-centred cubic unit cell is a cubic cell with an atom on each corner, and an atom at the centre of each _____.
e: Face-centred cubic cells have additional atoms located at the centre of each face.

q: A body-centred cubic unit cell is a cubic cell with an atom on each corner and another in the _____ of the cube.
e: Body-centred cubic cells feature one additional atom situated at the very centre of the cube.

q: The electrostatic attraction resulting from the opposite charges constitutes _____ bonds.
e: Ionic bonds are formed by the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

q: Covalent bonding usually occurs between _____.
e: Covalent bonding typically occurs between non-metal atoms.

q: A covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of the atoms and the _____ electrons.
e: Covalent bonds involve the electrostatic attraction between nuclei and shared valence electrons.

q: When hydrogen atoms are approaching, there is a repulsive force between the electrons since like charges _____.
e: Electrons carry like negative charges, which causes them to repel each other.

q: There is an optimum distance between two nuclei called the bond length where net attractive forces are _____.
e: The bond length represents the distance where net attractive forces are maximised and the molecule is most stable.

q: In single covalent bonds, only _____ pair of electrons is shared between two atoms.
e: A single covalent bond involves the sharing of exactly one pair of electrons.

q: A double bond is formed by sharing _____ pairs of electrons between two atoms.
e: A double covalent bond consists of two shared electron pairs.

q: The higher the number of bonded electrons, the stronger the attraction and the _____ the bond length.
e: More shared electrons increase the attractive force, pulling nuclei closer and shortening the bond length.

q: The bond length of the single bond is the longest, followed by the double bond and _____ bond.
e: Triple bonds have the shortest bond length among single, double, and triple covalent bonds.

q: The bond strength of the _____ bond is the highest, followed by the double bond and single bond.
e: Triple bonds possess the highest bond strength due to the sharing of three electron pairs.

q: A coordinate bond is characterised by the fact that the two shared electrons are both donated by _____ of the participating atoms.
e: In a coordinate bond, a single atom donates both electrons to be shared.

q: A coordinate bond is formed when one of the participating atoms possesses an unshared pair of electrons known as a _____.
e: Coordinate bonds require a lone pair of electrons to be donated.

q: A coordinate bond is expressed as an arrow which indicates the direction in which the electrons are _____.
e: The arrow in a coordinate bond points from the donor atom to the acceptor atom.

q: The ammonia molecule possesses a lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom; it can be donated to a hydrogen ion to produce the _____ ion.
e: Ammonia reacting with a hydrogen ion forms the ammonium ion ($NH_4^+$).

q: A water molecule can react with a hydrogen ion through a coordinate bond, giving a _____ ion.
e: Water donating a lone pair to $H^+$ forms the hydronium ion ($H_3O^+$).

q: Molecules with incomplete octets are called _____ molecules.
e: Molecules where the central atom has fewer than 8 valence electrons are electron-deficient.

q: An ammonia molecule can combine with boron trifluoride using a coordinate bond to form an _____.
e: The product of a coordinate bond between $NH_3$ and $BF_3$ is known as an adduct.

q: In carbon monoxide, the CO molecule has a triple bond that consists of two covalent bonds and one _____ bond.
e: Carbon monoxide contains a triple bond comprising two standard covalent bonds and one coordinate bond.

q: In drawing Lewis structures, for ions, it is necessary to add electrons to account for negative charges, and _____ electrons to account for positive charges.
e: Positive charges indicate a loss of electrons, so electrons must be subtracted from the total count.

q: The central atom in an electron-deficient molecule has valence electrons of less than _____.
e: Electron-deficient molecules feature a central atom with fewer than 8 valence electrons.

q: The central atom in an expanded valence shell molecule has valence electrons of more than _____.
e: Expanded valence shell molecules contain a central atom surrounded by more than 8 electrons.

q: The molecular shape can be predicted by using the Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory, also known as the _____ model.
e: VSEPR theory is the standard model used to predict molecular geometry.

q: The repulsive interaction of electron pairs increases in the order of bonding pair-bonding pair < lone pair-bonding pair < _____.
e: Lone pairs occupy more space, making lone pair-lone pair repulsion the strongest.

q: The lone pairs of electrons in a molecule occupy _____ space compared with the bonding pairs of electrons.
e: Because they are not shared, lone pairs spread out more and occupy greater space.

q: A triatomic molecule ($AX_2$ type) with only two bonding pairs without lone pairs has a _____ shape.
e: An $AX_2$ molecule with no lone pairs adopts a linear geometry.

q: In the $CO_2$ molecule, there are four bonding pairs (two double bonds) without lone pairs, hence the shape of $CO_2$ is _____.
e: Carbon dioxide has a linear shape due to the symmetrical arrangement of its double bonds.

q: The $AX_3$ type molecule without lone pairs has a _____ shape.
e: Molecules with three bonding pairs and no lone pairs are triangular planar.

q: The $AX_2E$ type molecule, where E represents a lone pair, has a _____ shape.
e: The presence of one lone pair in an $AX_2E$ system forces the molecule into a bent shape.

q: The $AX_4$ type molecule without lone pairs has a _____ shape.
e: Four bonding pairs with no lone pairs arrange themselves tetrahedrally.

q: The $AX_3E$ type molecule has a _____ shape.
e: Three bonding pairs and one lone pair result in a trigonal pyramidal geometry.

q: In a diamond, each carbon atom is joined to _____ other carbon atoms by strong covalent bonds.
e: Diamond features a giant structure where every carbon is bonded to four others.

q: In the case of graphite, each layer is formed with _____ rings of carbon atoms.
e: Graphite layers consist of interlocking hexagonal rings of carbon atoms.

q: There are weak _____ forces between the layers of graphite.
e: Weak van der Waals forces hold the separate layers of graphite together.

q: In contrast to diamond, graphite has free-moving electrons in each layer, that is why graphite can conduct _____.
e: Delocalised electrons in graphite layers allow it to conduct electricity.

q: Silicon(IV) oxide, $SiO_2$, is an example of a giant _____ molecule.
e: Silicon(IV) oxide forms a giant covalent structure similar to diamond.

q: If the atoms in a covalent bond are not identical, the electrons will not be equally shared, resulting in bond _____.
e: Unequal sharing of electrons due to electronegativity differences creates bond polarity.

q: The atom with the greater share of the electrons will be slightly negative and the other atom will be slightly positive, known as a _____.
e: A separation of partial charges within a bond creates a dipole.

q: Depending on the difference in electronegativity, covalent bonds can be polar or _____.
e: Covalent bonds are classified as polar or non-polar based on electron sharing.

q: The bond becomes more polar as the difference in electronegativity values of the atoms in a covalent bond _____.
e: Greater electronegativity differences lead to more unequal sharing and higher polarity.

q: In a covalent bond formed between two similar non-metal atoms, the shared electron pair is equally attracted resulting in a _____ covalent bond.
e: Identical atoms share electrons equally, forming non-polar covalent bonds.

q: The degree of bond polarity is measured as a _____ of a bond.
e: Dipole moment is the quantitative measure of bond polarity.

q: Any non-polar covalent bond has a _____ dipole moment.
e: Because electrons are shared equally, non-polar bonds have a dipole moment of zero.

q: In the case of polyatomic molecules, the dipole moment of a molecule is the _____ sum of the dipole moments of various bonds.
e: Molecular dipole moments are calculated as the vector sum of individual bond dipoles.

q: The $H_2O$ molecule has a bent shape and the total dipole moment is not zero, so it is a _____ molecule.
e: The asymmetrical bent shape of water prevents dipoles from cancelling, making it polar.

q: In the $CO_2$ molecule, the two equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel the effect of each other, thus it is a _____ molecule.
e: The linear symmetry of $CO_2$ causes bond dipoles to cancel, resulting in a non-polar molecule.

q: Van der Waals forces are weak forces which include dipole-dipole interaction, ion-dipole interaction, and _____ forces.
e: London dispersion forces are the third category of van der Waals forces.

q: Dipole-dipole interactions are formed when two _____ molecules interact with each other in space.
e: Dipole-dipole forces occur specifically between polar (dipolar) molecules.

q: Ion-dipole interaction is formed from the interaction between an ion and a _____ molecule.
e: Ion-dipole forces require an ion and a polar (dipole) molecule.

q: The weakest intermolecular forces that can be formed between atoms as well as non-polar molecules are known as _____ forces.
e: London dispersion forces are the weakest IMF and are present in all atoms and molecules.

q: Because of the constant motion of the electrons, an atom can develop a _____ dipole when the electrons are distributed unsymmetrically.
e: Random electron movement creates fleeting temporary dipoles.

q: London dispersion forces are also called induced dipole-_____ interaction.
e: A temporary dipole induces a dipole in a neighbouring atom, forming an induced dipole-induced dipole interaction.

q: Due to London dispersion forces, non-polar substances can condense into liquids and can freeze into solids when the temperature is lowered, such as liquid nitrogen and dry ice which is solid _____.
e: Dry ice is the solid form of carbon dioxide ($CO_2$).

q: The formation of hydrogen bonds requires the first molecule to have hydrogen attached to a high electronegative atom such as F, O, or _____.
e: Hydrogen bonding requires H to be bonded to Fluorine, Oxygen, or Nitrogen.

q: A hydrogen bond is a special type of dipole-dipole interaction and is the _____ of all intermolecular forces.
e: Hydrogen bonds are the strongest class of intermolecular forces.

q: In a metallic bond, the valence electrons of the atoms are very loosely held, forming a common _____ cloud.
e: Metallic bonding involves a shared cloud of delocalised valence electrons.

q: These mobile electrons in metallic bonding are often described as a "sea of _____".
e: The delocalised valence electrons are commonly referred to as a sea of electrons.

q: The positively charged metallic nuclei are surrounded by _____ electrons.
e: The sea of electrons in a metal is free to move throughout the lattice.

q: Metals consist of giant structures of atoms that are packed closely together in a regular arrangement called a _____.
e: Metal atoms form a closely packed regular arrangement known as a lattice.

q: The strength of metallic bonding increases with the increasing positive charge on the ions in the metal _____.
e: Higher ionic charges in the metal lattice lead to stronger electrostatic attractions.

q: The strength of metallic bonding increases with the _____ size of metal ions in the lattice.
e: Smaller metal ions bring the nuclei closer to the sea of electrons, increasing bond strength.

q: The strength of metallic bonding increases with the increasing number of _____ electrons per atom.
e: More mobile valence electrons contributed per atom strengthen the metallic bond.

q: The strength of metallic bond is _____ than that of an ionic bond.
e: Generally, metallic bonds are weaker and have lower bond strengths than ionic bonds.

q: Consequently, the melting points of some metals become _____ compared with the ionic compounds.
e: Because metallic bonds are generally weaker than ionic bonds, many metals have lower melting points than ionic solids.

q: The bonding in metals results from the interaction of the mobile electrons with the various nuclei, hence they are held together by a strong _____ attraction.
e: Metallic bonding relies on the electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and negative delocalised electrons.
